name: The Peter Principle
statement: In a hierarchy, every employee tends to rise to his level of incompetence.
statementAccent: rise to his level of incompetence
meaning: Promotion rewards being good at the job you already have, not the job you are moving into. So people keep getting promoted until they land in a role they are bad at — and there they stop, and stay.
example: The best engineer on the team is made engineering manager. The skills that earned the promotion — deep focus, solving it herself — are the ones she must now stop using. She is a mediocre manager, so she is never promoted again, and the team has lost its best engineer twice over.
whyItMatters: If the only route to more money and status runs through management, you will convert your best specialists into your worst managers. Parallel tracks, trial periods with an honest route back, and promoting on evidence of the next job rather than mastery of the last one are the standard defences.
origin: Laurence J. Peter formulated the principle; the 1969 book The Peter Principle was written up with the playwright Raymond Hull. It was framed as satire, but has since found real empirical support: Benson, Li and Shue's study of sales workers at 131 firms found that firms did promote on current sales performance, that the best salespeople made measurably worse managers, and that the resulting mismatch was costly.

sources.text: Peter, L.J., & Hull, R. (1969). The Peter Principle: Why Things Always Go Wrong. New York: William Morrow and Company.

Benson, A., Li, D., & Shue, K. (2019). "Promotions and the Peter Principle." The Quarterly Journal of Economics, 134(4), 2085–2134. — the published version of record, which reports a sample of 131 firms. Note: the superseded NBER working-paper draft (No. 24343, February 2018) reported 214 firms, and that stale figure is still repeated by the NBER landing page and by Wikipedia. Cite the 131 of the published paper.
